---
title: "Study 1 (Hive): Engagement, misinformation, and emotional language"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    df-print: paged
    fig-width: 8
    fig-height: 5
editor: visual
---

This document runs the complete Study 1 analysis in a fixed narrative order. Section 1 builds every variable in one place, confirmatory and exploratory alike, so all later sections draw on identical constructions. Section 2 describes the sample. Section 3 screens the seven candidate engagement outcomes with t-tests. Section 4 shows the correlation structure across outcomes and predictors, after which the final set of dependent variables is fixed. Section 5 verifies that the within-author comparisons are genuinely identified. Section 6 answers the confirmatory questions (H1 and H2). Section 7 asks what actually drives engagement on Hive and decomposes the author effect. Section 8 takes the promised closer look at emotional language dispersion, valence dynamics, and political identity references, and documents the exclusion of the outrage classifier. Section 9 collects robustness checks.

All language about results is associative rather than causal, in line with an observational field design. Models use `feols`; standard errors are heteroskedasticity robust (HC1) and not clustered, because author is absorbed as a fixed effect in the key comparison column. Engagement outcomes are logged with `log1p` because the raw counts are right skewed; for reblogs, where roughly three quarters of posts have none, the primary specification is the extensive margin (any reblog vs none) with the logged count as companion.

# 0. Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)       # data handling and plots
library(readxl)          # read the .xlsx dataset
library(janitor)         # clean column names
library(fixest)          # regressions with fixed effects
library(modelsummary)    # regression tables
library(gt)              # table objects + PDF export
library(ggcorrplot)      # correlation heatmap
library(marginaleffects) # predictions and per-level slopes
library(arrow)           # parquet files (exploratory variables)
# NOTE: car is intentionally not attached; car::recode() would mask dplyr::recode().
rm(list = ls()); set.seed(20260101)

# ---- paths ------------------------------------------------------------------
base_dir  <- "C:\\Users\\batuh\\PycharmProjects\\Thesis\\fact_checked_hive_pipeline"
data_path <- file.path(base_dir, "6. regression",              "hive_regression_dataset.xlsx")
dyn_path  <- file.path(base_dir, "9. Sentence Emotion Scoring", "hive_emotion_dynamics_filtered.parquet")
pol_path  <- file.path(base_dir, "10. Political Identity Language", "hive_political_identity.parquet")
pf_path   <- file.path(base_dir, "12. Post Features",           "hive_post_features.parquet")
std_path  <- file.path(base_dir, "12. Post Features",           "hive_author_standing.parquet")

fig_dir <- "figures";        dir.create(fig_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
pdf_dir <- "regression_pdfs"; dir.create(pdf_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
save_pdf <- TRUE   # PDF export needs webshot2 + Chrome/Chromium

# ---- inference --------------------------------------------------------------
# HC1 robust, NO clustering. Author is absorbed as a fixed effect in column 4.
se_main <- "hetero"

# ---- shared look ------------------------------------------------------------
acc_cols <- c("Accurate" = "#2166AC", "Misinformation" = "#B2182B")
theme_pres <- function(base = 12)
  theme_minimal(base_size = base) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.title.position = "plot",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "top")
save_fig <- function(name, w = 7, h = 4.5)
  ggsave(file.path(fig_dir, name), width = w, height = h, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

# 1. Data and variables

Every variable used anywhere in this document is built here, in one pass, so the confirmatory and exploratory sections cannot drift apart. Two measurement facts are stated up front because they matter for reading later tables. First, the confirmatory emotional language variable (`emo_z`) is the post-level score from the chunk-and-average DistilRoBERTa pipeline, while the exploratory mean (`emean_z`) is the average of sentence-level scores after boilerplate filtering; the two correlate at about .72 and are related but not identical quantities, so their coefficients are never compared directly. Second, valence dispersion and valence volatility correlate at .84 in this corpus, so they are treated as alternative operationalisations of one construct (valence movement) and never enter the same model, mirroring the rule already applied to the emotional language family (dispersion retained, volatility as variant, r = .82).

## 1.1 Core variables

```{r}
#| label: build-core
data <- read_xlsx(data_path) |> clean_names()
num  <- function(x) suppressWarnings(readr::parse_number(as.character(x)))

emo6    <- c("anger", "disgust", "fear", "joy", "sadness", "surprise")
eng_raw <- c("payout", "net_votes", "comments", "reblogs", "downvotes",
             "distinct_voters", "upvotes")

# Logged engagement outcomes + the extensive margin for reblogs
data <- data |>
  mutate(across(all_of(eng_raw), num)) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(eng_raw), ~ log1p(pmax(.x, 0)), .names = "log_{.col}"),
         any_reblog = as.integer(reblogs > 0))

# Emotions and emotional language: raw values here; standardisation happens
# after the analysis sample is fixed, so coefficients read per SD of the
# sample actually analysed.
data <- data |>
  mutate(across(all_of(c(emo6, "neutral", "emotional_language")), num))

# Accuracy, controls, fixed-effect keys, author-standing snapshots
data <- data |>
  mutate(misinformation        = num(misinformation),        # 1 = misinformation
         misinformation_strict = num(misinformation_strict),
         log_len       = num(log_len),
         is_political  = num(is_political),
         month         = as.factor(month),
         author        = as.character(author),
         label_source  = as.character(label_source))
# NOTE: the scrape-time snapshots reputation_ui, effective_vesting, and
# post_count are NOT used anywhere. They describe accounts as of January
# 2025, not as of the observation window, and reputation is partly built
# from the rewards of the posts under study. Author standing enters via
# strictly pre-window measures reconstructed from HiveSQL operation
# tables (joined in section 1.2b).

# Five-level accuracy scale (ref = true); bare 'misinformation' labels fold into 'false'
lvl5    <- c("pants_on_fire", "false", "mostly_false", "mostly_true", "true")
to_acc5 <- function(fl) {
  fl <- tolower(trimws(as.character(fl)))
  dplyr::case_when(fl %in% lvl5 ~ fl, fl == "misinformation" ~ "false",
                   TRUE ~ NA_character_)
}
data <- data |>
  mutate(accuracy_5 = fct_relevel(factor(to_acc5(final_label), levels = lvl5), "true"))

# ---- analysis sample, then standardisation ----------------------------------
model_data <- data |>
  filter(analysis_sample == TRUE, !is.na(emotional_language), !is.na(log_len)) |>
  mutate(category = fct_infreq(factor(category)),
         emo_z    = as.numeric(scale(emotional_language)),
         across(all_of(emo6), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x)), .names = "{.col}_z"))

cat("Analysis sample:", nrow(model_data),
    "| unique authors:", n_distinct(model_data$author), "\n")
cat("Misinformation flag:\n"); print(table(model_data$misinformation))
cat("Five levels (note the small pants_on_fire cell):\n")
print(table(model_data$accuracy_5, useNA = "ifany"))
cat("\nShare of posts with zero reblogs:",
    round(100 * mean(model_data$reblogs == 0, na.rm = TRUE), 1), "%\n")
```

## 1.2 Exploratory variables (sentence dynamics, political references, format)

These come from three sources built outside this document: sentence-level emotional dynamics scored with the same DistilRoBERTa classifier plus VADER for valence, after boilerplate filtering; political identity-reference counts adapted from the dictionaries of Rathje et al. (2021), counted overall because the in-group vs out-group contrast requires author political identity, which is unknown for Hive authors; and post format features from the January 2025 scrape. A fourth extension, the moral outrage classifier of Brady et al. (2021), was made operational but excluded after a manual validity audit (documented in section 8.6); no outrage variable enters any model.

```{r}
#| label: build-exploratory
#| message: false
dyn <- read_parquet(dyn_path) |>
  mutate(.key = as.character(doc_id)) |>
  select(.key, n_sentences_kept, n_sentences_dropped,
         emo_lang_mean, emo_lang_sd, emo_lang_volatility,
         vader_compound_mean, vader_compound_sd, vader_compound_volatility)
pol <- read_parquet(pol_path) |>
  mutate(.key = as.character(doc_id)) |>
  select(.key, pol_total, pol_log1p, pol_density100, pol_any)
pf  <- read_parquet(pf_path) |>
  mutate(.key = as.character(doc_id)) |>
  select(.key, n_images, n_links, n_tags, is_weekend, post_hour)

model_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(.key = as.character(doc_id)) |>
  left_join(dyn, by = ".key") |>
  left_join(pol, by = ".key") |>
  left_join(pf,  by = ".key")

cat("Joined:", sum(!is.na(model_data$pol_total)), "political,",
    sum(!is.na(model_data$emo_lang_mean)), "dynamics,",
    sum(!is.na(model_data$n_images)), "format rows of", nrow(model_data), "\n")

# Standardised once on the analysis sample so every coefficient reads per SD
# of the same sample. Skewed counts enter as log1p before scaling.
model_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(emean_z    = as.numeric(scale(emo_lang_mean)),
         esd_z      = as.numeric(scale(emo_lang_sd)),
         evol_z     = as.numeric(scale(emo_lang_volatility)),
         vmean_z    = as.numeric(scale(vader_compound_mean)),
         vsd_z      = as.numeric(scale(vader_compound_sd)),
         vvol_z     = as.numeric(scale(vader_compound_volatility)),
         pol_z      = as.numeric(scale(pol_log1p)),
         pol_dens_z = as.numeric(scale(pol_density100)),
         img_z      = as.numeric(scale(log1p(n_images))),
         lnk_z      = as.numeric(scale(log1p(n_links))),
         tags_z     = as.numeric(scale(log1p(n_tags))),
         hour_f     = as.factor(post_hour))

# Dynamics sample: dispersion/volatility need at least three usable sentences.
exp_dyn <- model_data |> filter(!is.na(vader_compound_volatility),
                                !is.na(emo_lang_volatility))
cat("Dynamics sample:", nrow(exp_dyn),
    "(", nrow(model_data) - nrow(exp_dyn), "excluded, too few sentences )\n")

# Dictionary validity, one line: political posts should mention identity
# terms far more often than non-political posts.
cat("Any political identity mention | political:",
    round(mean(model_data$pol_any[model_data$is_political == 1], na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    "| non-political:",
    round(mean(model_data$pol_any[model_data$is_political == 0], na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")
```

## 1.2b Author standing, strictly pre-window (HiveSQL reconstruction)

Author standing is measured from HiveSQL operation tables, which are append-only histories, using only operations dated before 2024-09-01. Each measure is therefore exact as of the window start and cannot mechanically contain the rewards of any post in the sample. Four measures enter: cumulative author rewards (the standing proxy replacing reputation, which has no historical snapshots and cannot be credibly reconstructed), cumulative curation rewards (a stake-activity proxy, since curation earnings scale with the Hive Power an account actually votes with), lifetime root-post count, and account age at window start. Authors created after the window start carry meaningful zeros.

```{r}
#| label: build-standing
#| message: false
standing <- read_parquet(std_path) |>
  transmute(author = as.character(author),
            log_pre_rewards  = log1p(pmax(as.numeric(pre_author_rew_vests), 0)),
            log_pre_curation = log1p(pmax(as.numeric(pre_curation_vests), 0)),
            log_pre_posts    = log1p(pmax(as.numeric(pre_root_posts), 0)),
            log_acct_age     = log1p(pmax(as.numeric(acct_age_days), 0)))

model_data <- model_data |> left_join(standing, by = "author")

std_vars <- c("log_pre_rewards", "log_pre_curation", "log_pre_posts", "log_acct_age")
cat("Standing coverage:",
    sum(complete.cases(model_data[std_vars])), "of", nrow(model_data),
    "posts have all four measures\n")
cat("Authors with zero pre-window author rewards:",
    round(100 * mean(model_data$log_pre_rewards == 0, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    "% of posts\n")
```

# 2. What the sample looks like

Descriptive only and unadjusted; any gap here can reflect topic, length, or author rather than accuracy or emotion. The adjusted models are the evidence.

```{r}
#| label: desc-shared
acc5_order <- c("pants_on_fire", "false", "mostly_false", "mostly_true", "true")
acc5_labs  <- c("Pants on fire", "False", "Mostly false", "Mostly true", "True")
acc5_cols  <- c("Pants on fire" = "#B2182B", "False" = "#D6604D",
                "Mostly false" = "#F4A582", "Mostly true" = "#92C5DE", "True" = "#2166AC")
grp_of <- function(x) ifelse(x == 1, "Misinformation", "Accurate")
```

**Accuracy labels.** The class balance, and how rare the most extreme category is.

```{r}
#| label: desc-accuracy
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
comp <- model_data |>
  filter(!is.na(accuracy_5)) |>
  mutate(lab = factor(as.character(accuracy_5), levels = acc5_order, labels = acc5_labs)) |>
  count(lab) |> mutate(pct = n / sum(n))
ggplot(comp, aes(n, lab, fill = lab)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%d  (%.1f%%)", n, 100 * pct)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = acc5_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Accuracy labels across the sample",
       subtitle = sprintf("%s labelled posts; pants on fire is rare",
                          format(nrow(model_data), big.mark = ",")),
       x = "Number of posts", y = NULL) +
  theme_pres(11)
save_fig("desc_accuracy_distribution.png", w = 8, h = 4)
```

**Emotional profile.** Misinformation leans more to anger and disgust, less to joy; this motivates the discrete-emotion decomposition in section 6.2.

```{r}
#| label: desc-emotion-profile
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
emo7 <- c(emo6, "neutral")
emo_prof <- model_data |>
  mutate(grp = grp_of(misinformation)) |>
  group_by(grp) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(emo7), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(emo7), names_to = "emotion", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(emotion = tools::toTitleCase(emotion))
ord <- emo_prof |> group_by(emotion) |> summarise(m = mean(share)) |> arrange(m) |> pull(emotion)
emo_prof <- emo_prof |> mutate(emotion = factor(emotion, levels = ord))
ggplot(emo_prof, aes(share, emotion)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = emotion), color = "grey75", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(color = grp), size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = acc_cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Emotional profile of posts",
       subtitle = "Average share of each emotion by accuracy group",
       x = "Average share of post emotion", y = NULL) +
  theme_pres(11)
save_fig("desc_emotion_profile.png", w = 7.5, h = 4.5)
```

**Engagement across the five levels (unadjusted).** Engagement is roughly flat across most accuracy levels and falls only at pants_on_fire, whose interval is wide because the cell is small.

```{r}
#| label: desc-accuracy5-means
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
acc5_summ <- model_data |>
  filter(!is.na(accuracy_5)) |>
  mutate(acc5 = factor(as.character(accuracy_5), levels = acc5_order, labels = acc5_labs)) |>
  select(acc5, log_net_votes, log_reblogs) |>
  pivot_longer(c(log_net_votes, log_reblogs), names_to = "outcome", values_to = "eng") |>
  filter(is.finite(eng)) |>
  group_by(outcome, acc5) |>
  summarise(n = n(), m = mean(eng), se = sd(eng) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(lo = m - 1.96 * se, hi = m + 1.96 * se,
         outcome = dplyr::recode(outcome,
                          log_net_votes = "Net votes",
                          log_reblogs   = "Reblogs (log count)"))
ggplot(acc5_summ, aes(acc5, m)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), color = "#B2182B") +
  facet_wrap(~outcome, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Engagement across the five accuracy levels (unadjusted)",
       subtitle = "Means with 95% intervals",
       x = NULL, y = "log(1 + outcome)") +
  theme_pres(11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))
save_fig("accuracy5_means.png", w = 9, h = 4)
```

# 3. Screening the candidate outcomes (t-tests)

Eight engagement outcomes are candidates. Each is tested for a mean difference between misinformation and accurate posts, on the logged scale (for the binary any-reblog outcome the t-test is a two-sample comparison of proportions). The same test is then applied to the emotion variables as a descriptive profile. The screen is transparent input to the outcome decision, not the decision itself: dropping outcomes solely because a t-test is non-significant would be a form of outcome selection, so the final choice in section 4 combines this screen with theory and redundancy.

```{r}
#| label: tt-helper
tt_table <- function(vars) {
  rows <- lapply(vars, function(v) {
    a <- model_data |> filter(misinformation == 1) |> pull(!!sym(v))
    b <- model_data |> filter(misinformation == 0) |> pull(!!sym(v))
    a <- a[is.finite(a)]; b <- b[is.finite(b)]
    tt <- t.test(a, b)
    data.frame(Variable = v,
               Mean_misinfo = mean(a), Mean_accurate = mean(b),
               Diff = mean(a) - mean(b),
               t_stat = unname(tt$statistic), p_value = tt$p.value,
               CI_low = tt$conf.int[1], CI_high = tt$conf.int[2])
  })
  bind_rows(rows) |>
    mutate(across(c(Mean_misinfo, Mean_accurate, Diff, t_stat, CI_low, CI_high),
                  ~ round(.x, 3)),
           p_value = round(p_value, 3))
}
```

# 4. Correlation structure and the final outcome set

One heatmap over all candidate outcomes, confirmatory variables, and exploratory variables, on natural scales. Two kinds of strong correlation are expected and mechanical: the sentence-based mean and dispersion derive from the same scores, and each volatility correlates highly with its own dispersion (r = .82 for emotional language, .84 for valence), which is why the dispersion and volatility of a family never enter the same model. Among the outcomes, upvotes and distinct voters correlate near 1 with net votes because downvotes are rare, and payout is computed from the rshares that votes allocate, so it moves with net votes by construction.

```{r}
#| label: table-D-corr
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 10
cor_vars <- model_data |>
  transmute(log_payout, log_net_votes, log_upvotes, log_distinct_voters,
            log_comments, log_reblogs, any_reblog, log_downvotes,
            misinformation, emotional_language,
            emo_mean = emo_lang_mean, emo_disp = emo_lang_sd,
            emo_vol = emo_lang_volatility,
            val_mean = vader_compound_mean, val_disp = vader_compound_sd,
            val_vol = vader_compound_volatility,
            pol_refs = pol_log1p,
            images = log1p(n_images), links = log1p(n_links),
            tags = log1p(n_tags), weekend = is_weekend,
            log_len, is_political) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))
M <- cor(cor_vars, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
p_corr <- ggcorrplot(M, type = "full", lab = TRUE, lab_size = 1.6, tl.cex = 8,
                     colors = c("#6BAED6", "white", "#FB6A4A"),
                     title = "Correlations: candidate outcomes, confirmatory and exploratory variables")
p_corr
ggsave(file.path(pdf_dir, "D_correlations.png"), p_corr, width = 11, height = 10, dpi = 300)
```

**Misinformation and the discrete emotions.** Point-biserial correlations of the binary flag with each emotion dimension. These are expectedly small even where the regressions find real differences, because a single correlation compresses the relationship without conditioning on topic or time; the emotion profile in section 2 and Table B in section 6 are the informative views.

```{r}
#| label: misinfo-emotion-cor
tibble(variable = c(emo6, "neutral", "emotional_language"),
       r_with_misinformation = map_dbl(
         c(emo6, "neutral", "emotional_language"),
         ~ cor(model_data$misinformation, model_data[[.x]],
               use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))) |>
  mutate(r_with_misinformation = round(r_with_misinformation, 3)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(r_with_misinformation)))
```

## 4.1 The final dependent variables

```{r}
#| label: final-dvs
r_nv <- function(v) round(cor(model_data$log_net_votes, model_data[[v]],
                              use = "pairwise.complete.obs"), 3)
cat("Redundancy with net votes: upvotes r =", r_nv("log_upvotes"),
    "| distinct voters r =", r_nv("log_distinct_voters"),
    "| payout r =", r_nv("log_payout"), "\n")
cat("Redundancy within diffusion: any_reblog vs log_reblogs r =",
    round(cor(model_data$any_reblog, model_data$log_reblogs,
              use = "pairwise.complete.obs"), 3), "\n\n")

dv_all <- c(log_net_votes = "Net votes",
            any_reblog    = "Any reblog")
keep_dvs <- names(dv_all)

cat("Retained outcomes:\n")
cat(paste0(" - ", keep_dvs, " (", dv_all[keep_dvs], ")"), sep = "\n")
cat("\nExcluded or demoted, with reason:\n",
    " - log_upvotes, log_distinct_voters: redundant approval copies of net votes (r near 1)\n",
    " - log_payout: mechanically downstream of votes (computed from allocated rshares)\n",
    " - log_reblogs: r = .88 with any_reblog; with ~73% zeros the log count mostly\n",
    "   re-expresses the zero vs nonzero boundary; kept as a robustness companion (9.5)\n",
    " - log_comments, log_downvotes: secondary margins; no accuracy difference in the screen\n")
```

The retained pair maps onto the two margins the research question names. Net votes is the tokenized action: on Hive an upvote allocates real rewards from the stake-weighted pool, so approval is precisely where a reward-driven amplification of misinformation would have to appear. Any reblog is diffusion, the margin central to the misinformation literature. Because roughly three quarters of posts have zero reblogs and the observed counts span only about twenty distinct values, the binary extensive margin carries essentially all the diffusion information, which the .88 correlation with the log count confirms; the log-count model is therefore reported once, as a robustness companion in section 9.5, rather than duplicated through every main table.

# 5. Identification: can the within-author column speak?

The key comparison in every table below is column 4, which adds author fixed effects and identifies coefficients only from variation within authors. This section verifies that this variation exists, so that the within-author estimates can be read as genuine findings rather than artifacts of absorbed variation.

```{r}
#| label: within-author-check
# Who provides the within-author identifying variation for the binary flag?
auth_var <- model_data |>
  group_by(author) |>
  summarise(n_posts    = n(),
            n_misinfo  = sum(misinformation == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_accurate = sum(misinformation == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
            mixed      = n_misinfo > 0 & n_accurate > 0, .groups = "drop")
auth_var |>
  summarise(authors            = n(),
            multi_post_authors = sum(n_posts >= 2),
            mixed_authors      = sum(mixed),
            posts_in_mixed     = sum(n_posts[mixed])) |>
  print()

# Residual variation after author demeaning (multi-post authors only):
demean_stats <- model_data |>
  group_by(author) |> filter(n() >= 2) |>
  mutate(inter = misinformation * emo_z,
         across(c(misinformation, emo_z, inter), ~ .x - mean(.x), .names = "w_{.col}")) |>
  ungroup() |>
  summarise(across(starts_with("w_"), sd))
cat("\nWithin-author SDs (misinformation, emotional language, interaction):\n")
print(demean_stats)

# Mixed authors: real emotional-language spread across their two label groups?
mixed_check <- model_data |>
  group_by(author) |>
  filter(n_distinct(misinformation) == 2) |>
  summarise(sd_emo  = sd(emo_z),
            emo_gap = abs(mean(emo_z[misinformation == 1]) -
                          mean(emo_z[misinformation == 0])), .groups = "drop")
cat("\nMixed authors:", nrow(mixed_check),
    "| with real emotional-language spread (sd > 0.25):",
    sum(mixed_check$sd_emo > 0.25, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
cat("Emotional-language gap between an author's accurate and misinformation posts:\n")
print(summary(mixed_check$emo_gap))

# Five-level accuracy: how thin is the within-author variation per label?
cat("\nPosts per level inside authors who vary across levels (5-level caution):\n")
model_data |>
  filter(!is.na(accuracy_5)) |>
  group_by(author) |> filter(n_distinct(accuracy_5) >= 2) |> ungroup() |>
  count(accuracy_5, name = "posts_in_varying_authors") |>
  print()
```

Reading: the within-author variation is broad, not residual. For a binary flag with roughly one-third prevalence the raw SD is about .47, and .39 of it survives author demeaning; about .72 SD of emotional language and .48 of the interaction remain within authors. Most mixed authors show real spread in emotional language across their accurate and misinformation posts, so the within-author estimates of all three confirmatory terms rest on well-distributed variation. The five-level within-author cells are much thinner, which is why the five-level author column in section 6.3 is read more cautiously than the binary one.

# 6. Confirmatory analysis: H1 and H2

## 6.0 Shared regression machinery

Each family is built up over four columns: (1) the bare terms, (2) plus post-level controls (`log_len`, `is_political`), (3) plus category and month fixed effects, the core adjusted model, and (4) author fixed effects, the within-author comparison. The pre-window author-standing measures from section 1.2b are deliberately not controls in the confirmatory ladder: the confirmatory question is whether accuracy and emotional language are associated with engagement, and standing is a channel through which author identity operates rather than a post-level confounder to hold fixed. Standing enters in section 7, where the question changes to what the author effect is made of.

```{r}
#| label: reg-helpers
ctrl    <- "log_len + is_political"
fe_main <- "category + month"
fe_auth <- "category + month + author"
emoB    <- paste(paste0(emo6, "_z"), collapse = " + ")
gof_drop <- "AIC|BIC|Log.Lik|RMSE|Std.Errors|R2 Adj|R2 Pseudo|^F$"

cmap <- c(
  "misinformation"                = "Misinformation",
  "emo_z"                         = "Emotional language (z)",
  "misinformation:emo_z"          = "Misinformation x Emo. language",
  "anger_z"                       = "Anger (z)",
  "disgust_z"                     = "Disgust (z)",
  "fear_z"                        = "Fear (z)",
  "joy_z"                         = "Joy (z)",
  "sadness_z"                     = "Sadness (z)",
  "surprise_z"                    = "Surprise (z)",
  "misinformation:anger_z"        = "Misinformation x Anger",
  "misinformation:disgust_z"      = "Misinformation x Disgust",
  "misinformation:fear_z"         = "Misinformation x Fear",
  "misinformation:joy_z"          = "Misinformation x Joy",
  "misinformation:sadness_z"      = "Misinformation x Sadness",
  "misinformation:surprise_z"     = "Misinformation x Surprise",
  "accuracy_5pants_on_fire"       = "Pants on fire",
  "accuracy_5false"               = "False",
  "accuracy_5mostly_false"        = "Mostly false",
  "accuracy_5mostly_true"         = "Mostly true",
  "accuracy_5pants_on_fire:emo_z" = "Pants on fire x Emo. language",
  "accuracy_5false:emo_z"         = "False x Emo. language",
  "accuracy_5mostly_false:emo_z"  = "Mostly false x Emo. language",
  "accuracy_5mostly_true:emo_z"   = "Mostly true x Emo. language",
  "log_len"                       = "log(length)",
  "is_political"                  = "Political"
)

fit_specs <- function(dv, base, data = model_data) {
  f <- function(rhs, fe = NULL)
    feols(as.formula(paste0(dv, " ~ ", rhs, if (!is.null(fe)) paste0(" | ", fe))),
          data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
  list("(1)"                 = f(base),
       "(2) + controls"      = f(paste0(base, " + ", ctrl)),
       "(3) + controls + FE" = f(paste0(base, " + ", ctrl), fe_main),
       "(4) + author FE"     = f(paste0(base, " + ", ctrl), fe_auth))
}
famA <- function(dv) fit_specs(dv, "misinformation*emo_z")
famB <- function(dv) fit_specs(dv, paste0("misinformation*(", emoB, ")"))
famC <- function(dv) fit_specs(dv, "accuracy_5*emo_z",
                               data = model_data |> filter(!is.na(accuracy_5)))

show_family <- function(fam, dv, tag, code, map = cmap) {
  tab <- modelsummary(fam(dv), stars = TRUE, coef_map = map, gof_omit = gof_drop,
                      output = "gt", title = paste0(tag, " - ", dv_all[[dv]]))
  if (save_pdf) {
    f <- file.path(pdf_dir, paste0(code, "_", sub("^log_", "", dv), ".pdf"))
    tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tab, f),
             error = function(e) message("Could not write ", f, ": ",
                                         conditionMessage(e)))
  }
  tab
}
```

## 6.1 Table A. Misinformation x emotional language

The reading: the raw misinformation penalty in column 1 shrinks under controls and vanishes under category and month fixed effects, so the apparent penalty reflects what misinformation posts tend to be about, not their accuracy. The emotional language coefficient strengthens from column 1 to 2 because the bare estimate mixes a positive emotional-language association with a penalty on political content; unbundling them reveals the positive association for accurate posts. The negative interaction means emotional language shows no comparable gain for misinformation. In column 4, everything is indistinguishable from zero: within authors, neither accuracy nor emotional language moves engagement.

```{r}
#| label: tableA
for (dv in keep_dvs) print(show_family(famA, dv, "Table A", "A"))
```

## 6.2 Table B. Which emotion carries the interaction?

The decomposition into six discrete emotions shows the negative interaction of Table A is almost entirely an anger interaction: emotionally angry misinformation is associated with fewer net votes, while the other five emotion interactions are null. This connects to the excluded outrage classifier (section 8.6): outrage could not be measured directly, but anger, its nearest available dimension, is exactly where the misinformation interaction concentrates.

```{r}
#| label: tableB
for (dv in keep_dvs) print(show_family(famB, dv, "Table B", "B"))
```

```{r}
tabB_slide <- modelsummary(
  list(
    "(3) core adjusted" = famB("log_net_votes")[[3]],
    "(4) author FE"     = famB("log_net_votes")[[4]]
  ),
  stars = TRUE,
  coef_map = cmap[c(
    "anger_z",
    "misinformation:anger_z",
    "misinformation:disgust_z",
    "misinformation:fear_z",
    "misinformation:joy_z",
    "misinformation:sadness_z",
    "misinformation:surprise_z"
  )],

)
```

## 6.3 Table C. The five accuracy levels

The five-level view shows the sharp engagement drop is confined to pants_on_fire, and the companion below reports, for all five levels, the adjusted level and the emotional-language slope inside each label from the column 3 model. Note the slope pattern: the emotional language premium lives in mostly_true posts and is absent for fully true ones, which suggests the premium attaches to opinionated but broadly accurate commentary as a genre rather than to accuracy itself. The five-level author-FE column is read cautiously given the thin within-author cells documented in section 5.

```{r}
#| label: tableC
for (dv in keep_dvs) print(show_family(famC, dv, "Table C", "C"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tableC-companion
acc_companion <- function(dv) {
  m  <- famC(dv)[["(3) + controls + FE"]]
  nd <- model_data |> filter(!is.na(accuracy_5))
  slp <- avg_slopes(m, variables = "emo_z", by = "accuracy_5", newdata = nd) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    transmute(accuracy_5 = as.character(accuracy_5),
              emo_slope = estimate, emo_slope_se = std.error, emo_slope_p = p.value)
  prd <- avg_predictions(m, by = "accuracy_5", newdata = nd, vcov = FALSE) |>
    as_tibble() |>
    transmute(accuracy_5 = as.character(accuracy_5), adj_mean = estimate)
  left_join(prd, slp, by = "accuracy_5") |>
    mutate(accuracy_5 = factor(accuracy_5, levels = acc5_order, labels = acc5_labs)) |>
    arrange(accuracy_5)
}
comp_nv <- acc_companion("log_net_votes")
print(comp_nv)

# Figure: the per-label emotional-language slope, the H2 story in one panel.
comp_nv |>
  mutate(lo = emo_slope - 1.96 * emo_slope_se,
         hi = emo_slope + 1.96 * emo_slope_se) |>
  ggplot(aes(emo_slope, accuracy_5)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.2, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#1F4E79") +
  labs(title = "Emotional-language slope by accuracy label (net votes)",
       subtitle = "Column 3 model; per SD of emotional language, 95% intervals",
       x = "Slope on log(net votes + 1)", y = NULL) +
  theme_pres(11)
save_fig("figC_per_label_slopes.png", w = 7, h = 4)
```

## 6.4 Figures: the confirmatory story at a glance

The coefficient ladder shows the three confirmatory terms across the four specifications; the interaction plot shows the surviving column 3 finding; the binned scatter makes the within-author null visible rather than merely stated.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ladder
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7
tidy_ladder <- function(fam_list, terms) {
  purrr::imap_dfr(fam_list, function(m, nm) {
    ct <- as.data.frame(fixest::coeftable(m)); ct$term <- rownames(ct)
    ct |>
      filter(term %in% terms) |>
      transmute(spec = nm, term, estimate = Estimate, se = `Std. Error`,
                p = `Pr(>|t|)`, lo = estimate - 1.96 * se, hi = estimate + 1.96 * se)
  })
}
plot_ladder <- function(fam, dv, term_labels, title, code) {
  d <- tidy_ladder(fam(dv), names(term_labels)) |>
    mutate(term_label = factor(term_labels[term], levels = unname(term_labels)),
           spec = factor(spec, levels = rev(unique(spec))), sig = p < .05)
  g <- ggplot(d, aes(estimate, spec)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey55") +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.18,
                   linewidth = 0.45, colour = "grey35") +
    geom_point(aes(fill = sig), shape = 21, size = 2.7, colour = "grey20", stroke = 0.4) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#1F4E79", `FALSE` = "white"),
                      labels = c(`TRUE` = "p < .05", `FALSE` = "n.s."), name = NULL) +
    facet_wrap(~ term_label, scales = "free_x") +
    labs(title = paste0(title, " - ", dv_all[[dv]]),
         subtitle = "Point estimates with 95% intervals across specifications (1) to (4)",
         x = "Coefficient", y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9),
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), legend.position = "bottom")
  print(g)
  ggsave(file.path(pdf_dir, paste0(code, "_", sub("^log_", "", dv), "_coefplot.png")),
         g, width = 11, height = 7, dpi = 300)
  invisible(g)
}
labs_A <- c("misinformation"       = "Misinformation",
            "emo_z"                = "Emotional language (z)",
            "misinformation:emo_z" = "Misinfo x Emo. language")
for (dv in keep_dvs) plot_ladder(famA, dv, labs_A, "Figure A. Confirmatory ladder", "figA")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-interaction

# marginaleffects cannot propagate uncertainty for ABSORBED fixed effects,

ggplot(plot_data,

  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
```

```{r}
within_d <- model_data |>
```

## 6.5 What section 6 establishes

H1 is not supported at any layer. The raw penalty in column 1 is composition; the adjusted estimate is indistinguishable from zero and robust to the Poisson functional form (section 9.1); the within-author estimate is a precise null resting on the well-verified variation of section 5; and the diffusion outcome is null throughout, with the log-count companion (section 9.5) showing the same, so misinformation is not reblogged more. H2 is partially contradicted in an informative direction: emotional language is associated with more approval only for broadly accurate content, the penalty for emotional misinformation is specifically an anger penalty, and the premium concentrates in mostly_true posts. Both patterns are between-author patterns that vanish within authors, and the asymmetry appears only in approval, the tokenized action that allocates rewards, not in diffusion, which carries no direct reward. Whether that between-author asymmetry reflects content or the authors behind it is the question section 7 answers.

# 7. What drives engagement on Hive

## 7.1 Engagement follows authors

```{r}
#| label: author-dominance
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
share_out <- c(log_net_votes = "Net votes", log_reblogs = "Reblogs",
               log_payout = "Payout", log_comments = "Comments",
               log_downvotes = "Downvotes")
var_share_author <- function(v) {
  d <- model_data |> select(author, all_of(v)) |>
    rename(y = !!sym(v)) |> filter(is.finite(y))
  grand <- mean(d$y); sst <- sum((d$y - grand)^2)
  ssb <- d |> group_by(author) |>
    summarise(n = n(), m = mean(y), .groups = "drop") |>
    summarise(ssb = sum(n * (m - grand)^2)) |> pull(ssb)
  ssb / sst
}
auth_share <- tibble(label = unname(share_out),
                     share = map_dbl(names(share_out), var_share_author)) |>
  mutate(label = fct_reorder(label, share))
ggplot(auth_share, aes(share, label)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4C72B0", width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 1)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "Share of engagement variance explained by author identity",
       subtitle = "One-way decomposition by author; the remainder is within-author variation",
       x = "Between-author share of variance", y = NULL) +
  theme_pres(11)
save_fig("author_variance_share.png", w = 7, h = 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: engagement-concentration
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5
auth_eng <- model_data |>
  group_by(author) |>
  summarise(eng = sum(pmax(net_votes, 0), na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(eng)
ev <- auth_eng$eng; nA <- length(ev)
gini <- (2 * sum(seq_len(nA) * ev) / (nA * sum(ev))) - (nA + 1) / nA
lor  <- tibble(cum_authors = seq_len(nA) / nA, cum_eng = cumsum(ev) / sum(ev))
ggplot(lor, aes(cum_authors, cum_eng)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(color = "#B2182B", linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.04, y = 0.92, hjust = 0,
           label = sprintf("Gini = %.2f", gini), fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "A few authors receive most of the engagement",
       subtitle = "Cumulative share of net votes across authors; dashed line is equality",
       x = "Cumulative share of authors", y = "Cumulative share of net votes") +
  theme_pres(11)
save_fig("desc_engagement_concentration.png", w = 6.5, h = 5)
```
