## 7.2 Isolating the author-FE contribution (same-sample check)

Columns 3 and 4 of Table A differ in sample as well as specification: single-post authors drop out under author fixed effects. Re-running column 3 on the column 4 sample separates the two. The result is diagnostic: the emotional language main effect already fades on the restricted sample, so its column 3 strength is carried substantially by single-appearance authors, while the interaction survives the restriction and dies only when author effects enter, making it a genuinely between-author pattern among multi-post authors.

```{r}
#| label: same-sample
f_col3 <- log_net_votes ~ misinformation * emo_z + log_len + is_political | category + month
f_col4 <- log_net_votes ~ misinformation * emo_z + log_len + is_political | category + month + author
m3f <- feols(f_col3, data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
m4f <- feols(f_col4, data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
col4_sample <- model_data[obs(m4f), ]
m3_sub <- feols(f_col3, data = col4_sample, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
tabR1 <- modelsummary(
  list("(3) full sample" = m3f, "(3) col-4 sample" = m3_sub, "(4) author FE" = m4f),
  stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = cmap[c("misinformation", "emo_z", "misinformation:emo_z", "log_len")],
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared", "r2.within"),
  title = "Table R1. Isolating the author-FE contribution (net votes)")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabR1, file.path(pdf_dir, "R1_same_sample.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabR1
```

## 7.3 Decomposing the author effect: pre-window standing

The four pre-window standing measures are added to the core model. Because every measure is built exclusively from operations dated before the observation window, none can mechanically contain the rewards of the posts under study, which removes the bad-control problem the scrape-time snapshots had. The quantity of interest is how far R2 moves from column 3 toward the author-FE ceiling: the movement measures how much of the author effect is captured by observable pre-window standing, and the remaining gap reflects other observed or unobserved author-level heterogeneity, such as network position, community ties, stable content quality, audience, or habitual style. One interpretive caution remains and is milder than before: pre-window standing reflects stable author quality and past success, so the (3b) misinformation and emotional-language coefficients are still read as descriptive adjustments rather than cleaner effect estimates. The individual standing coefficients are likewise not interpreted singly, because they are mutually conditional (for example, root-post count and account age enter net of accumulated rewards, so they capture reward-per-post efficiency rather than posting or tenure as such); the decomposition rests on the joint R2 movement, not on any one sign.

```{r}
#| label: stake-standing
m3b <- feols(log_net_votes ~ misinformation * emo_z + log_len + is_political +
               log_pre_rewards + log_pre_curation + log_pre_posts +
               log_acct_age | category + month,
             data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
tabR2 <- modelsummary(
  list("(3) core" = m3f, "(3b) + pre-window standing" = m3b, "(4) author FE" = m4f),
  stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = c(cmap[c("misinformation", "emo_z", "misinformation:emo_z")],
               "log_pre_rewards"  = "log(pre-window author rewards)",
               "log_pre_curation" = "log(pre-window curation rewards)",
               "log_pre_posts"    = "log(pre-window root posts)",
               "log_acct_age"     = "log(account age, days)"),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared", "r2.within"),
  title = "Table R2. How much of the author effect is pre-window standing?",
  notes = "Standing measured strictly before the observation window from HiveSQL operation tables; it cannot contain the sampled posts' own rewards. The (3b) accuracy and emotional-language coefficients remain descriptive.")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabR2, file.path(pdf_dir, "R2_stake_standing.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabR2
```

Reading: the four pre-window standing measures move R2 from .151 to .597, accounting for roughly 60 percent of the additional explanatory power between the core model and the author fixed-effect specification; the remaining gap reflects other observed or unobserved author-level heterogeneity. The decline of the emotional language main effect from .107 to .008 indicates substantial overlap between the between-author emotional language association and pre-existing standing; the standing-adjusted coefficient is not read as a cleaner effect estimate. The interaction is the one confirmatory term that survives standing adjustment (-.103) before vanishing within authors, so the accuracy asymmetry is a between-author pattern but not merely a standing pattern. The individual standing coefficients are not read singly, as noted above; in particular the negative conditional signs on root posts and account age reflect reward-per-post efficiency given accumulated rewards, not any penalty to posting or tenure.

## 7.4 Composition placebo: the author profile of misinformation posts

If the raw misinformation penalty is composition, the authors behind misinformation and accurate posts should differ in pre-window standing, and regressing the standing measures on the misinformation flag compares exactly that. Because standing is built only from operations dated before the window, the sampled posts cannot influence these measures, so pre-determination holds by construction. Two limits on interpretation apply nonetheless: this is a post-level composition analysis rather than an author-level analysis of misinformation propensity, and prolific authors contribute more observations, so the estimates are weighted toward active accounts. Positive coefficients therefore say that misinformation posts in this analysis sample are associated with higher-standing authors; they do not establish that established authors are more inclined to produce misinformation.

```{r}
#| label: placebo
plc <- list(
  "log(pre-window author rewards)"   =
    feols(log_pre_rewards  ~ misinformation | category + month,
          data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE),
  "log(pre-window curation rewards)" =
    feols(log_pre_curation ~ misinformation | category + month,
          data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE),
  "log(pre-window root posts)"       =
    feols(log_pre_posts    ~ misinformation | category + month,
          data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE),
  "log(account age)"                 =
    feols(log_acct_age     ~ misinformation | category + month,
          data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE))
tabR3 <- modelsummary(plc, stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = c("misinformation" = "Misinformation"),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"),
  title = "Table R3. Author composition placebo (pre-window standing)",
  notes = "Standing measured strictly before the observation window; pre-determined by construction. Positive coefficients indicate that misinformation posts in this analysis sample come from authors with higher pre-window standing; the estimates describe post-level author composition, not author-level misinformation propensity.")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabR3, file.path(pdf_dir, "R3_placebo.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabR3
```

Reading: misinformation posts in the analysis sample are associated with authors who have more pre-window author rewards, more prior root posts, and older accounts; curation rewards show no difference, which is coherent because curation tracks voting activity rather than authorship. The pattern may partly reflect greater posting exposure among prolific accounts, and the sampling gate selects claim-bearing political and current-events content that established accounts produce more of. What the result does support is a composition statement: misinformation in this sample is not confined to new or marginal accounts. It is a statement about origin, not intent or propensity. Whether any accounts deliberately exploit standing to spread inaccurate content profitably cannot be established from post-level field data; section 7.4b tests the observable implications, and the question otherwise requires experimental or account-level longitudinal designs and is left to future research.

## 7.4b Does misinformation pay? Payout and standing heterogeneity (exploratory)

Two observable implications of a strategic-monetization account can be tested. First, if misinformation is financially rewarded, misinformation posts should earn higher payouts; payout was excluded as a primary outcome because it is mechanically downstream of votes, but for this targeted question it is exactly the right variable. Second, if established accounts specifically can monetize misinformation, the misinformation association should turn positive at high pre-window standing, which an interaction with pre-window author rewards tests. Both models are exploratory and read with the same caution as everything in this section. Note the within-author null of Table A already constrains the strategic story: mixed authors' misinformation does not outperform their own accurate posts, so any strategic mechanism would have to operate at the account level rather than the post level.

```{r}
#| label: payout-heterogeneity
famPay <- famA("log_payout")
m_het  <- feols(log_net_votes ~ misinformation * log_pre_rewards + emo_z +
                  log_len + is_political | category + month,
                data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
tabR4 <- modelsummary(
  list("Payout (3)" = famPay[["(3) + controls + FE"]],
       "Payout (4)" = famPay[["(4) + author FE"]],
       "Net votes: standing heterogeneity (3)" = m_het),
  stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = c("misinformation"                  = "Misinformation",
               "emo_z"                           = "Emotional language (z)",
               "misinformation:emo_z"            = "Misinformation x Emo. language",
               "log_pre_rewards"                 = "log(pre-window author rewards)",
               "misinformation:log_pre_rewards"  = "Misinformation x Pre-window rewards"),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared", "r2.within"),
  title = "Table R4. Payout and standing heterogeneity (exploratory)",
  notes = "Payout is mechanically downstream of votes and is used here only for this targeted question. The heterogeneity model asks whether the misinformation association differs by pre-window standing.")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabR4, file.path(pdf_dir, "R4_payout_heterogeneity.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabR4
```

Reading: if the payout estimates are null in both columns and the heterogeneity interaction is null, the monetary version of the amplification hypothesis is closed at every observable margin, and the strategic-account question is framed honestly as future research with a policy observation: content moderation on stake-weighted platforms should not assume misinformation comes from new or peripheral accounts. If the heterogeneity interaction is positive and credible, it is reported as an exploratory finding with explicit multiple-testing caution and no causal language.

## 7.5 What section 7 establishes

Author identity absorbs the large majority of engagement variance, and a substantial share of that author effect is accounted for by observable pre-window standing in the stake-weighted system. Misinformation posts in the sample are associated with authors of higher pre-window standing (more accumulated author rewards, more prior posts, older accounts; curation rewards show no difference), so the raw between-author comparison mixes a standing premium with whatever accuracy response exists. Together these results give the platform-mechanism reading of the confirmatory nulls: engagement on Hive is more strongly associated with accumulated author standing than with the measured post-level content features.

# 8. Exploratory analysis: dispersion, valence, and identity language

Three questions promised a closer look, each with its own subsection and a consistent format: the family alone, columns 3 and 4 side by side, one reading paragraph. Two bridge diagnostics (E4 and E5) then connect the emotional-dynamics measures directly back to the confirmatory Table A, separating what changes because of the smaller dynamics sample, the sentence-level measurement, and the addition of movement or valence. A compact figure at the end shows the between-vs-within contrasts at a glance. The volatility measures follow the sentiment volatility formula of Berger et al. (2021), the standard deviation of differences between adjacent segments; the valence version adapts their construct directly, since their measure is defined over sentiment, while the emotional-language version transfers the same logic to a different dimension, and in both cases the segment is the sentence, a finer unit than the 500-word chunks and paragraphs used in the original. Dispersion (the standard deviation of the scores themselves) and volatility are conceptually distinct, because dispersion ignores the ordering of sentences, but they are statistically inseparable in this corpus (r = .82 for emotional language, .84 for valence), so each model uses one of the pair; agreement across the two variants supports that a result is not an artifact of a single operationalisation.

## 8.1 Emotional language: mean vs movement

```{r}
#| label: e1-dispersion
famE1   <- fit_specs("log_net_votes", "emean_z + esd_z",  data = exp_dyn)
famE1v  <- fit_specs("log_net_votes", "emean_z + evol_z", data = exp_dyn)
famE1r  <- fit_specs("any_reblog",    "emean_z + esd_z",  data = exp_dyn)
famE1rv <- fit_specs("any_reblog",    "emean_z + evol_z", data = exp_dyn)
tabE1 <- modelsummary(
  list("NV, dispersion (3)" = famE1[[3]],   "NV, dispersion (4)" = famE1[[4]],
       "NV, volatility (3)" = famE1v[[3]],  "NV, volatility (4)" = famE1v[[4]],
       "AR, dispersion (3)" = famE1r[[3]],  "AR, dispersion (4)" = famE1r[[4]],
       "AR, volatility (3)" = famE1rv[[3]], "AR, volatility (4)" = famE1rv[[4]]),
  stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = c("emean_z" = "Emotional language mean (z)",
               "esd_z"   = "Emotional language dispersion (z)",
               "evol_z"  = "Emotional language volatility (z)"),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r2.within"),
  title = "Table E1. Mean vs movement of emotional language (alternative operationalisations)",
  notes = "NV = net votes, AR = any reblog. Sentence-level measures (related to but distinct from the post-level confirmatory variable, r = .72). Dispersion is the standard deviation of sentence scores; volatility is the standard deviation of differences between consecutive sentence scores, the sentiment volatility formula of Berger et al. (2021) applied to emotional language at the sentence level. The two are conceptually distinct but correlate at .82 here and are fit separately; agreement across variants supports that the associations are not artifacts of a single operationalisation. Columns (3): controls + category and month FE. Columns (4): author FE.")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabE1, file.path(pdf_dir, "E1_dispersion.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabE1
```

Reading: across both movement operationalisations, greater emotional-language movement is positively associated with net votes between authors, and conditional on movement, a higher average emotional-language level is negatively associated with net votes. The agreement across variants supports that this is not an artifact of a single measurement choice. All estimates are null under author fixed effects, which suggests the associations primarily reflect differences in authors' typical writing styles rather than a within-author post-level advantage that a writer could act on.

## 8.2 Valence: level and movement

```{r}
#| label: e2-valence
famV_d  <- fit_specs("log_net_votes", "vmean_z + vsd_z",  data = exp_dyn)
famV_v  <- fit_specs("log_net_votes", "vmean_z + vvol_z", data = exp_dyn)
famV_dr <- fit_specs("any_reblog",    "vmean_z + vsd_z",  data = exp_dyn)
tabE2 <- modelsummary(
  list("NV, dispersion (3)" = famV_d[[3]],  "NV, dispersion (4)" = famV_d[[4]],
       "NV, volatility (3)" = famV_v[[3]],  "NV, volatility (4)" = famV_v[[4]],
       "Any reblog (3)"     = famV_dr[[3]], "Any reblog (4)"     = famV_dr[[4]]),
  stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = c("vmean_z" = "Valence mean (z)",
               "vsd_z"   = "Valence dispersion (z)",
               "vvol_z"  = "Valence volatility (z)"),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r2.within"),
  title = "Table E2. Valence level and movement (alternative operationalisations)",
  notes = "NV = net votes. Valence volatility is the standard deviation of adjacent-sentence differences in VADER compound scores, the direct sentence-level adaptation of the sentiment volatility measure of Berger et al. (2021). Dispersion and volatility correlate at .84 and are fit separately; agreement across variants supports that the associations are not artifacts of a single operationalisation.")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabE2, file.path(pdf_dir, "E2_valence.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabE2
```

Reading: the valence mean shows a small positive within-author association that is stable across operationalisations: when an author writes more positively than their own baseline, that post does slightly better. That the association appears under author fixed effects rather than dying there is interpretable: between authors, valence is entangled with author style and topic (it correlates -.41 with the political flag), and demeaning strips that confound, leaving a small clean within signal. The movement measures are negative for diffusion between authors and null within; where the dispersion and volatility variants disagree, no claim is made.

## 8.3 Table E4. Does emotional-language movement change the original Table A result?

E1 reports the standalone associations of the sentence-level measures. This section asks the bridge question: does the confirmatory Table A pattern change once the emotional-dynamics measurement enters, and if so, at which step? Three steps are separated, all on the common dynamics sample (`exp_dyn`) so that every model within a comparison uses identical rows. Model 1 reruns the exact Table A specification on the dynamics sample, isolating pure sample restriction. Model 2 replaces the chunk-and-average confirmatory score (`emo_z`) with the boilerplate-filtered sentence-level mean (`emean_z`), isolating the measurement change; the two scores target the same construct (emotional vs neutral language, not valence) but correlate at only .72. Models 3 and 4 then add dispersion or volatility as explanatory variables, in alternative specifications because the two movement measures correlate at .82; no misinformation interactions with movement are added, since the question is whether the original misinformation-by-emotional-language pattern survives the presence of movement, not whether a new interaction exists. These are exploratory diagnostic comparisons, not new confirmatory hypotheses, and all language is associative.

```{r}
#| label: e4-bridge
mapE4 <- c(
  "misinformation"          = "Misinformation",
  "emo_z"                   = "Emotional language, chunk-based (z)",
  "misinformation:emo_z"    = "Misinfo x Emo. language (chunk)",
  "emean_z"                 = "Emotional language, sentence mean (z)",
  "misinformation:emean_z"  = "Misinfo x Emo. language (sentence mean)",
  "esd_z"                   = "Emotional language dispersion (z)",
  "evol_z"                  = "Emotional language volatility (z)",
  "log_len"                 = "log(length)")

noteE4 <- paste(
  "All models on the common dynamics sample (exp_dyn).",
  "Model 1 isolates the effect of restricting Table A to the dynamics sample.",
  "Model 2 isolates the change from the original chunk-based score to the sentence-level mean (r = .72 between the two).",
  "Models 3 and 4 test whether adding dispersion or volatility changes the original interaction pattern;",
  "they are alternative specifications because the two movement measures correlate at .82.",
  "HC1 standard errors.")

e4_fams <- function(dv) list(
  "(1) Table A spec"     = fit_specs(dv, "misinformation*emo_z",             data = exp_dyn),
  "(2) Sentence mean"    = fit_specs(dv, "misinformation*emean_z",           data = exp_dyn),
  "(3) + dispersion"     = fit_specs(dv, "misinformation*emean_z + esd_z",   data = exp_dyn),
  "(4) + volatility"     = fit_specs(dv, "misinformation*emean_z + evol_z",  data = exp_dyn))

bridge_panel <- function(fams, spec_name, title, tag, map, note) {
  mods <- lapply(fams, function(f) f[[spec_name]])
  tab <- modelsummary(mods, stars = TRUE, output = "gt", coef_map = map,
                      gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared", "r2.within"),
                      title = title, notes = note)
  if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tab, file.path(pdf_dir, paste0(tag, ".pdf"))),
                         error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
  tab
}

famsE4_nv <- e4_fams("log_net_votes")
famsE4_ar <- e4_fams("any_reblog")

bridge_panel(famsE4_nv, "(3) + controls + FE",
             "Table E4, Panel A. Net votes, specification (3)", "E4_A_netvotes_s3", mapE4, noteE4)
bridge_panel(famsE4_nv, "(4) + author FE",
             "Table E4, Panel B. Net votes, specification (4)", "E4_B_netvotes_s4", mapE4, noteE4)
bridge_panel(famsE4_ar, "(3) + controls + FE",
             "Table E4, Panel C. Any reblog, specification (3)", "E4_C_anyreblog_s3", mapE4, noteE4)
bridge_panel(famsE4_ar, "(4) + author FE",
             "Table E4, Panel D. Any reblog, specification (4)", "E4_D_anyreblog_s4", mapE4, noteE4)
```

\[PENDING FIRST RENDER\] Reading to be written from the rendered panels, answering, in order: (1) does the Table A misinformation-by-emotional-language interaction survive when Table A is rerun on the dynamics sample; (2) does replacing the chunk-based score with the sentence-level mean change the coefficient or its significance; (3) does adding dispersion materially move the misinformation, sentence-mean, or interaction coefficients; (4) does adding volatility; (5) do any apparent differences remain under author fixed effects. No claim that movement changes the Table A result will be made unless the coefficients move meaningfully in the rendered output.

## 8.4 Table E5. Do valence level and valence movement account for the original Table A pattern?

E4 varies the emotional-language measurement; E5 keeps the original Table A variables intact in every model and asks instead whether signed valence explains the pattern. Emotional language measures emotional vs neutral language and is unsigned; the VADER compound score measures positive-to-negative valence and is signed, so the two are conceptually distinct dimensions (they correlate at -.33 in this corpus). If the Table A emotional-language coefficients shrink once valence level or valence movement enters, the original pattern partly reflects valence rather than emotionality per se. The VADER volatility variable is the closer adaptation of Berger et al.'s (2021) original valence-based construct. No misinformation-by-valence interactions are added; the question is whether valence accounts for the existing pattern, not whether a new interaction exists. Dispersion and volatility again enter as alternatives (r = .84). All models on `exp_dyn`, associative language throughout.

```{r}
#| label: e5-bridge
mapE5 <- c(
  "misinformation"       = "Misinformation",
  "emo_z"                = "Emotional language (z)",
  "misinformation:emo_z" = "Misinformation x Emo. language",
  "vmean_z"              = "Valence mean (z)",
  "vsd_z"                = "Valence dispersion (z)",
  "vvol_z"               = "Valence volatility (z)",
  "log_len"              = "log(length)")

noteE5 <- paste(
  "All models on the common dynamics sample (exp_dyn); Table A variables retained throughout.",
  "VADER compound provides a signed sentence-level valence score from negative to positive:",
  "vmean_z is the average, vsd_z the dispersion of sentence scores without regard to order,",
  "and vvol_z the Berger-style volatility, the standard deviation of changes between consecutive sentence scores.",
  "Models 3 and 4 are alternative specifications because valence dispersion and volatility correlate at .84.",
  "The comparison tests whether valence level and movement account for the original Table A emotional-language coefficients.",
  "HC1 standard errors.")

e5_fams <- function(dv) list(
  "(1) Table A spec"   = fit_specs(dv, "misinformation*emo_z",                     data = exp_dyn),
  "(2) + valence mean" = fit_specs(dv, "misinformation*emo_z + vmean_z",           data = exp_dyn),
  "(3) + dispersion"   = fit_specs(dv, "misinformation*emo_z + vmean_z + vsd_z",   data = exp_dyn),
  "(4) + volatility"   = fit_specs(dv, "misinformation*emo_z + vmean_z + vvol_z",  data = exp_dyn))

famsE5_nv <- e5_fams("log_net_votes")
famsE5_ar <- e5_fams("any_reblog")

bridge_panel(famsE5_nv, "(3) + controls + FE",
             "Table E5, Panel A. Net votes, specification (3)", "E5_A_netvotes_s3", mapE5, noteE5)
bridge_panel(famsE5_nv, "(4) + author FE",
             "Table E5, Panel B. Net votes, specification (4)", "E5_B_netvotes_s4", mapE5, noteE5)
bridge_panel(famsE5_ar, "(3) + controls + FE",
             "Table E5, Panel C. Any reblog, specification (3)", "E5_C_anyreblog_s3", mapE5, noteE5)
bridge_panel(famsE5_ar, "(4) + author FE",
             "Table E5, Panel D. Any reblog, specification (4)", "E5_D_anyreblog_s4", mapE5, noteE5)
```

\[PENDING FIRST RENDER\] Reading to be written from the rendered panels, reporting, in order: (1) whether adding average valence changes the Table A misinformation, emotional-language, or interaction coefficients; (2) whether valence dispersion changes them further; (3) whether valence volatility changes them further; (4) whether the valence variables themselves remain associated with engagement under author fixed effects, where the E2 within-author valence-mean result gives the prior expectation; (5) whether the reading differs between net votes and any reblog. The final thesis conclusion is not revised until these panels are inspected.

## 8.5 Political identity references (Rathje et al., 2021)

```{r}
#| label: e3-political
famP  <- fit_specs("log_net_votes", "pol_z")
famPd <- fit_specs("log_net_votes", "pol_dens_z")
famPs <- fit_specs("log_net_votes", "pol_z",
                   data = model_data |> filter(is_political == 1))
tabE3 <- modelsummary(
  list("Count form (3)"     = famP[[3]],  "Count form (4)"     = famP[[4]],
       "Density form (3)"   = famPd[[3]], "Density form (4)"   = famPd[[4]],
       "Political only (3)" = famPs[[3]], "Political only (4)" = famPs[[4]]),
  stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = c("pol_z"      = "Political identity refs (z)",
               "pol_dens_z" = "Political identity refs, density (z)"),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r2.within"),
  title = "Table E3. Political identity references and approval (net votes)",
  notes = "Between-author estimates (columns 3) vary in sign across operationalisations; within-author estimates (columns 4) are consistently negative.")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabE3, file.path(pdf_dir, "E3_political.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabE3
```

Reading: the between-author association is fragile and specification-dependent, while the within-author association is consistently negative and modest, roughly a 3 to 4 percent decline in net votes per standard deviation of identity references. This pattern differs from the sharing premium for out-group language reported on centralized platforms (Rathje et al., 2021). Two platform features may contribute: Hive's feed is not engagement-optimised, so identity-charged content receives no algorithmic amplification, and stake-weighted votes deplete voting power and allocate real rewards, so an upvote is closer to a small payment than a costless reaction. A measurement caveat applies: the variable counts identity references overall, not out-group derogation specifically, so the construct overlap with Rathje et al. is partial.

## 8.6 The digital outrage classifier: a negative methods result

No code runs here by design. The Brady et al. (2021) classifier was validated on manually labelled Hive sentences and agreed on 29 of 30 non-outrage labels but only 7 of 30 outrage labels, with errors concentrated in gaming, technical, and everyday content that contains conflict vocabulary (attack, destroy, kill) without moral violation. This is a domain-transfer failure: the classifier was trained on US political Twitter and misreads Hive's platform culture, and Brady et al. themselves note that validity should be re-established when the tool is applied to new domains. The classifier was therefore excluded because it did not demonstrate adequate domain validity on Hive, and moral outrage is not measured directly in the present study. Anger is reported as a related but conceptually narrower emotion dimension: moral outrage in Brady et al.'s framework combines a perceived moral violation with anger, disgust, or contempt and an orientation toward blame, so the anger findings in Table B are informative about one component of the construct and are not treated as a substitute for it.

## 8.7 One figure for the section

```{r}
#| label: fig-explore-compact
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
pull_term <- function(m, term, spec, family) {
  ct <- as.data.frame(fixest::coeftable(m)); ct$t <- rownames(ct)
  ct <- ct[ct$t == term, ]
  if (!nrow(ct)) return(NULL)
  tibble(family, spec, estimate = ct$Estimate, se = ct$`Std. Error`)
}
comp <- bind_rows(
  pull_term(famE1[[3]], "esd_z",   "Between (col 3)", "Emo. language dispersion"),
  pull_term(famE1[[4]], "esd_z",   "Within (col 4)",  "Emo. language dispersion"),
  pull_term(famV_d[[3]], "vmean_z", "Between (col 3)", "Valence mean"),
  pull_term(famV_d[[4]], "vmean_z", "Within (col 4)",  "Valence mean"),
  pull_term(famP[[3]],  "pol_z",   "Between (col 3)", "Political identity refs"),
  pull_term(famP[[4]],  "pol_z",   "Within (col 4)",  "Political identity refs")) |>
  mutate(lo = estimate - 1.96 * se, hi = estimate + 1.96 * se)
ggplot(comp, aes(estimate, family, colour = spec)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.18,
                 position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Between (col 3)" = "#8DA9C4",
                                 "Within (col 4)"  = "#1F4E79"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Exploratory associations: between vs within authors",
       subtitle = "Net votes; 95% intervals; per SD of each predictor",
       x = "Coefficient (log net votes)", y = NULL) +
  theme_pres()
save_fig("figE_compact_between_within.png", w = 9, h = 4.5)
```

# 9. Robustness

Each check targets one named threat. Only the misinformation and interaction terms are displayed; full tables are written to `regression_pdfs/`.

## 9.1 Functional form: Poisson on raw counts

The log1p transformation is a modelling choice; Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood on the raw counts handles zeros natively and does not depend on it. Net votes cannot serve directly because it is upvotes minus downvotes and takes negative values on some posts, which the Poisson family does not allow, and dropping those posts would select on the outcome. Raw upvotes is a true nonnegative count that correlates near 1 with net votes because downvotes are rare, so the Poisson check runs on upvotes. Note `fepois` drops author groups whose outcome is all zeros in the FE column, so its N is slightly smaller.

```{r}
#| label: rob-poisson
cat("Posts with negative net votes:",
    sum(model_data$net_votes < 0, na.rm = TRUE), "of", nrow(model_data), "\n")
m3_pois <- fepois(upvotes ~ misinformation * emo_z + log_len + is_political |
                    category + month, data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
m4_pois <- fepois(upvotes ~ misinformation * emo_z + log_len + is_political |
                    category + month + author, data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
tabRob1 <- modelsummary(
  list("Poisson (3)" = m3_pois, "Poisson (4)" = m4_pois),
  stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = cmap[c("misinformation", "emo_z", "misinformation:emo_z")],
  gof_map = c("nobs"),
  title = "Table Rob1. Poisson PML on raw upvotes")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabRob1, file.path(pdf_dir, "Rob1_poisson.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabRob1
```

## 9.2 Measurement: strict labels and model3-only labels

Classification error in the pipeline labels attenuates coefficients toward zero, so the null is checked under the stricter label and under model3-only labels (excluding the 168 model1-fallback posts). The human validation study addresses the same threat from the annotation side.

```{r}
#| label: rob-labels
m3_strict <- feols(log_net_votes ~ misinformation_strict * emo_z + log_len +
                     is_political | category + month,
                   data = model_data |> filter(!is.na(misinformation_strict)),
                   vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
m3_model3 <- feols(f_col3, data = model_data |> filter(label_source == "model3"),
                   vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
tabRob2 <- modelsummary(
  list("(3) main" = m3f, "(3) strict labels" = m3_strict, "(3) model3 only" = m3_model3),
  stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = c("misinformation"               = "Misinformation",
               "misinformation_strict"        = "Misinformation (strict)",
               "emo_z"                        = "Emotional language (z)",
               "misinformation:emo_z"         = "Misinfo x Emo. language",
               "misinformation_strict:emo_z"  = "Misinfo (strict) x Emo. language"),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"),
  title = "Table Rob2. Label robustness (net votes)")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabRob2, file.path(pdf_dir, "Rob2_labels.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabRob2
```

## 9.3 Outliers: winsorized outcome

Hive engagement is heavy-tailed even after logging because stake-weighted whale votes concentrate approval. The outcome is winsorized at the 99th percentile; the null is more credible if it survives the outliers than if it depends on removing them, so this is a reported sensitivity, not a change to the primary specification.

```{r}
#| label: rob-winsor
wz <- function(x, p = 0.99) pmin(x, quantile(x, p, na.rm = TRUE))
m3_win <- feols(wz(log_net_votes) ~ misinformation * emo_z + log_len +
                  is_political | category + month,
                data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
tabRob3 <- modelsummary(
  list("(3) main" = m3f, "(3) winsorized 99%" = m3_win),
  stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = cmap[c("misinformation", "emo_z", "misinformation:emo_z")],
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"),
  title = "Table Rob3. Outlier sensitivity (net votes)")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabRob3, file.path(pdf_dir, "Rob3_winsor.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabRob3
```

## 9.4 Format controls: are the confirmatory estimates robust to presentation?

Weekend timing, tags, links, and images are not confirmatory controls by design: a control must plausibly confound, meaning it must correlate with both accuracy and engagement, and the correlation table shows the format features barely differ by accuracy (all \|r\| with misinformation below .05). Adding them also changes the estimand to the accuracy association net of presentation choices, which are part of the post the author composed rather than background conditions, and the confirmatory specification was fixed before the format features were built. The check yields a split result: the misinformation estimate is unchanged, confirming the H1 null is not sensitive to presentation, while the emotional language main effect and the interaction fall below significance once format enters. The between-author emotional language pattern therefore partly overlaps with presentation-rich posts, and it is reported with that qualifier; whether format features are confounders to remove or components of the authored content that should not be conditioned on is left as an open interpretive question.

```{r}
#| label: rob-format
m3_fmt <- feols(log_net_votes ~ misinformation * emo_z + log_len + is_political +
                  img_z + lnk_z + tags_z + is_weekend | category + month,
                data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
tabRob4 <- modelsummary(
  list("(3) main" = m3f, "(3) + format controls" = m3_fmt),
  stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = c(cmap[c("misinformation", "emo_z", "misinformation:emo_z")],
               "img_z"      = "Images (z)",
               "lnk_z"      = "Links (z)",
               "tags_z"     = "Tags (z)",
               "is_weekend" = "Weekend"),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"),
  title = "Table Rob4. Format-feature controls (net votes)")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabRob4, file.path(pdf_dir, "Rob4_format.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabRob4
```

## 9.5 Reblogs, intensive margin (log count companion)

The demoted log-count diffusion outcome, reported once for completeness. With \~73 percent zeros this model mostly re-expresses the extensive margin (r = .88 with any_reblog), which is why it is a companion rather than a main outcome.

```{r}
#| label: rob-reblogs-log
tabRob5 <- modelsummary(famA("log_reblogs"), stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = cmap[c("misinformation", "emo_z", "misinformation:emo_z", "log_len")],
  gof_omit = gof_drop,
  title = "Table Rob5. Reblogs, log count (companion to any reblog)")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabRob5, file.path(pdf_dir, "Rob5_reblogs_log.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabRob5
```

## 9.6 Period split (exploratory, read with caution)

The confirmatory model re-fit on pre-election (Sep-Oct), election (Nov), and post-election (Dec-Jan) subsamples. Three periods and three terms invite multiple comparisons and no correction is applied, so isolated significant cells are not treated as findings; the purpose is to show the confirmatory patterns are broadly stable across the election timeline. The five-level table and author effects are omitted because the split cells are too thin.

```{r}
#| label: rob-period
pd_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(period = dplyr::recode(as.character(month),
                                "2024-09" = "pre", "2024-10" = "pre",
                                "2024-11" = "election",
                                "2024-12" = "post", "2025-01" = "post"),
         period = factor(period, levels = c("pre", "election", "post")))
period_labs <- c(pre = "Pre (Sep-Oct)", election = "Election (Nov)", post = "Post (Dec-Jan)")
pmods <- lapply(names(period_labs), function(p)
  feols(f_col3, data = pd_data |> filter(period == p), vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE))
names(pmods) <- period_labs
tabRob6 <- modelsummary(pmods, stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = cmap[c("misinformation", "emo_z", "misinformation:emo_z")],
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"),
  title = "Table Rob6. Period split (net votes), exploratory")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabRob6, file.path(pdf_dir, "Rob6_period.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabRob6
```

## 9.7 Sign-preserving transformations of net votes

The primary outcome floors the 150 posts with negative net votes at zero before logging, since log1p is undefined below -1. Two transformations that preserve the sign and magnitude of negative values, the inverse hyperbolic sine and a signed log, check that this choice does not drive the confirmatory estimates.

```{r}
#| label: rob-transforms
model_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(asinh_net_votes = asinh(net_votes),
         slog_net_votes  = sign(net_votes) * log1p(abs(net_votes)))
m3_as <- feols(asinh_net_votes ~ misinformation * emo_z + log_len + is_political |
                 category + month, data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
m4_as <- feols(asinh_net_votes ~ misinformation * emo_z + log_len + is_political |
                 category + month + author, data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
m3_sl <- feols(slog_net_votes ~ misinformation * emo_z + log_len + is_political |
                 category + month, data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
m4_sl <- feols(slog_net_votes ~ misinformation * emo_z + log_len + is_political |
                 category + month + author, data = model_data, vcov = se_main, notes = FALSE)
tabRob7 <- modelsummary(
  list("asinh (3)" = m3_as, "asinh (4)" = m4_as,
       "signed log (3)" = m3_sl, "signed log (4)" = m4_sl),
  stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  coef_map = cmap[c("misinformation", "emo_z", "misinformation:emo_z")],
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared", "r2.within"),
  title = "Table Rob7. Sign-preserving outcome transformations (net votes)",
  notes = "asinh(x) and sign(x) * log(1 + |x|) retain the 150 negative net-vote values that the primary outcome floors at zero.")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabRob7, file.path(pdf_dir, "Rob7_transforms.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabRob7
```

## 9.8 Author-clustered standard errors (sensitivity)

The documented inference choice is HC1 without clustering, on the grounds that author is absorbed in the key comparison column. Absorbing the author mean does not by itself rule out residual correlation within authors, so the confirmatory family is re-reported with standard errors clustered by author as an appendix sensitivity. Point estimates are identical by construction; only the uncertainty changes.

```{r}
#| label: rob-cluster
tabRob8 <- modelsummary(famA("log_net_votes"), stars = TRUE, output = "gt",
  vcov = ~author,
  coef_map = cmap[c("misinformation", "emo_z", "misinformation:emo_z", "log_len")],
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared", "r2.within"),
  title = "Table Rob8. Table A (net votes) with author-clustered standard errors",
  notes = "Same models as Table A; standard errors clustered by author (1,716 clusters). Column (4) clusters on the fixed-effect dimension.")
if (save_pdf) tryCatch(gt::gtsave(tabRob8, file.path(pdf_dir, "Rob8_clustered.pdf")),
                       error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
tabRob8
```

# 10. Summary of the argument

Three layers, one story. Between all authors, misinformation appears penalized, but the penalty is composition: misinformation posts differ in topic and in who writes them, and the composition placebo, built on standing measured strictly before the window, shows misinformation posts are associated with higher-standing authors in the sample. Between multi-post authors, one asymmetry remains: emotional language is associated with more approval only for broadly accurate content, the penalty for emotional misinformation is specifically an anger penalty, and the asymmetry appears only in the tokenized approval margin, not in diffusion. Within authors, with identification verified in section 5, the estimates are precisely centred near zero. Author identity absorbs most engagement variance, and much of that author effect is observable pre-window standing in the stake-weighted system. The observational evidence therefore does not confirm the cobra effect: engagement on Hive is more strongly associated with accumulated author standing than with the measured post-level content features, and lower accuracy shows no observable engagement advantage at any margin, including payout. These statements are associative throughout: content accuracy is not exogenously assigned in field data, so causal effects of accuracy or emotional language on engagement remain a question for future experimental research.
